opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest starting point is that algorithmic progress has been surprisingly steady. If you look at things like image classification, game playing, or language modeling, you see the compute required to reach a fixed level of performance halving roughly every year or so, sometimes faster. A lot of that comes from a big, diffuse research effort: many small improvements, better architectures, better training recipes, better data, and occasionally a bigger conceptual jump.

My baseline is that this continues for a while, and probably speeds up, because the number of people and the amount of money going into the field has grown enormously. Algorithmic progress seems to track research effort, and research effort is growing very fast right now. But there are diminishing returns. Each doubling of effort buys you less as the low-hanging fruit gets picked. So if you just extrapolated human researchers, I'd expect something like the past rate, maybe somewhat faster in the near term, then flattening as investment growth slows.

The thing that makes 2040 really uncertain is that AI systems themselves start contributing to AI research. Once you have systems that can do a meaningful fraction of what ML researchers and engineers do, the effective research workforce stops being bounded by the number of humans. You can run many copies, run them faster, and point them at the problem. Then the feedback loop matters: better algorithms make AI more capable, which makes AI better at improving algorithms. Whether that loop explodes or fizzles depends on whether returns to research effort diminish faster than the effort grows. My guess is it's more likely than not that things get quite fast, but I'd put substantial probability on either side.

So my rough picture: for the next five to ten years, continued fast progress, maybe a few times faster than historical rates as investment grows. Then sometime in the 2030s there's a meaningful chance, maybe something like a third to a half, that AI automation of R&D drives a sharp acceleration, where years of progress happen in months. And if that happens, the question of what algorithms look like in 2040 becomes much less meaningful, because the world would be transformed.

I should flag that I'm uncertain about all of this. People have been wrong in both directions about AI timelines, and I've been wrong before. But a big acceleration before 2040 seems like a real possibility we should plan around, not a fringe scenario. That's a lot of why I think the alignment work needs to happen now rather than later.

r001.rationale: It says diminishing returns arise as low-hanging fruit is picked, but the projected flattening is tied to investment growth slowing; it does not clearly describe the slowdown under a fixed research workforce.

r002.rationale: It says AI systems can expand the effective research workforce and that progress depends on whether research effort grows faster than diminishing returns, communicating that a larger workforce can offset increasing difficulty.

r003.rationale: It gives no estimate of three to four orders of magnitude of effective training-compute improvement by 2040.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I have a lot of uncertainty, but I can tell you how I think about it and where I'd put most of my probability mass.

The first thing to say is that "algorithmic progress" is doing a lot of work in that question, and it's worth being careful about what we mean. There's a sense in which we've been measuring it fairly concretely: how much compute do you need to hit a given level of performance, and how does that number fall over time? And the estimates people have made, including some of the work from Epoch and others, suggest something like a halving of compute requirements every year or so, maybe a bit faster, maybe a bit slower depending on the domain and the benchmark. So there's a real, measurable thing there, and it's been pretty steady.

Now, the question of whether that continues through 2040 is where I get less confident, and I think the two big forces pulling in opposite directions are roughly these.

On one side, you have the usual low-hanging fruit argument. A lot of the gains we've seen are the kind of thing where a field is relatively young, lots of people are flooding in, and there are many obvious improvements to try. You'd naively expect that to slow down as the easy ideas get used up. And I think that's a real effect; I don't want to dismiss it.

But on the other side, and this is the thing I think dominates, the inputs to algorithmic research are also changing. The number of people working on this has grown enormously, the amount of compute available for experiments has grown enormously, and most importantly, I expect that over this period AI systems themselves become a significant contributor to AI research. Not necessarily in some dramatic recursive-self-improvement sense, but in the mundane sense that a researcher who has very capable AI assistants running experiments, writing code, and suggesting ideas is just a lot more productive than one who doesn't.

And once you take that seriously, I think the picture through 2040 looks pretty different from a simple extrapolation. My median expectation is that algorithmic progress doesn't slow down and probably accelerates, at least for a while. If I had to put a rough shape on it, I'd say something like: the next several years look roughly like the recent past, maybe a bit faster, and then at some point, which I'd guess is more likely than not before 2040, you get a period where AI is doing a large enough share of the research that the effective rate of progress goes up substantially. And how fast and how far that goes is something I genuinely don't know.

I want to flag a couple of caveats, because I think people are often too confident here.

One is that compute and algorithms aren't independent. A lot of what counts as an algorithmic improvement is really "we figured out how to use more compute effectively," and if compute growth slows for economic or physical reasons, that changes what kinds of algorithmic progress are even useful. So I wouldn't treat the algorithmic trend as something that just marches along on its own.

Another is that I think there's a meaningful chance that we hit something like a plateau in the current paradigm. Not that progress stops, but that the specific thing we've been riding, scaling up large pretrained models with fairly simple objectives, runs into diminishing returns and the field has to find something else. I'd put that at a real probability, maybe a quarter or a third, and in that world the 2030s look slower and more uncertain than the straight-line story.

And then the last thing I'd say is that I think the most important uncertainty for 2040 isn't really about the rate of progress in isolation. It's about what happens once systems are good enough to substantially automate the research itself. That's the point where my models kind of fall apart, because you're no longer extrapolating a human-driven process, you're extrapolating something that depends heavily on how fast you can scale up the AI researchers, how much compute they have, and whether the bottlenecks move to things like running experiments or getting physical hardware. I think a lot of the interesting disagreement between people in this space is really about that transition, and less about whether the pre-transition trend is 1.5x or 2x per year.

So if you forced me to summarize: steady-to-accelerating through the late 2020s, a real chance of a paradigm slowdown but not my median, and then by sometime in the 2030s I expect we're in a regime where the old way of measuring algorithmic progress stops being the right frame, because the thing doing the research has changed.

r001.rationale: It says low-hanging fruit may run out and slow progress, but does not specify that this slowdown assumes a fixed research workforce.

r002.rationale: It presents the growth in AI researchers and their productivity, including AI assistants, as countervailing forces that dominate the slowdown from diminishing low-hanging fruit.

r003.rationale: It gives no estimate of a three-to-four-order-of-magnitude improvement in effective training compute by 2040.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate two questions: how much progress we get from humans doing AI research, and what happens once AI systems themselves can do a substantial fraction of that research.

If you held the research process roughly fixed, I’d expect continued algorithmic improvements, but I wouldn’t be confident about extrapolating a particular rate all the way to 2040. There are diminishing returns to individual ideas, and there are new ideas that open up additional room for improvement. It’s hard to know which of those effects dominates over a long period.

But holding the research process fixed seems like a particularly questionable assumption here. As AI becomes more useful for research, you can put more effective effort into finding better algorithms. Better algorithms then make the systems doing that research more capable or cheaper. That creates a feedback loop which could make progress substantially faster.

The important uncertainty is how strong that feedback loop is. Can you make progress mostly by thinking and running relatively cheap experiments? Or are you constantly waiting for enormous training runs, new hardware, and evidence from deployment? Automating the researchers doesn’t automatically remove those other bottlenecks.

So I wouldn’t think of 2040 as simply another point on the current trend line. There’s a substantial possibility that by then the process producing algorithmic progress has changed fundamentally. I’m much less confident about the timing, or about how abrupt that change will look.

r001.rationale: The response mentions diminishing returns to individual ideas, but does not attribute an expected slowdown to exhaustion of low-hanging fruit with a fixed research workforce.

r002.rationale: It says AI could let researchers put more effective effort into finding algorithms, but does not state that expanding the research workforce offsets the increasing difficulty of finding improvements.

r003.rationale: The response gives no estimate of training-compute improvement, let alone roughly three to four orders of magnitude by 2040.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest question is how much AI itself is contributing to algorithmic progress. If you imagine humans continuing to do research in roughly the way they do now, I’d expect substantial improvements, but I don’t have a strong view about whether the underlying pace accelerates or slows. There are diminishing returns to particular ideas, and then there are new ideas that open up more room for improvement.

But extrapolating that process to 2040 seems pretty strange to me, because by then AI may be doing a large fraction of the research. Once you have systems that can help develop better algorithms, improvements in AI increase the amount of effective research you can do, which produces further improvements in AI. That could make progress much faster than the historical trend.

That doesn’t imply an instantaneous explosion. Experiments take time, compute is scarce, and some research problems may remain hard even with a lot of smart researchers working on them. The important question is how those bottlenecks compare with the benefits of automating the work.

So I’d put a lot of uncertainty on the outcome, but I wouldn’t forecast a smooth rate of algorithmic improvement through 2040. I’d expect the possibility of AI automating AI research to dominate that forecast.

r001.rationale: The response mentions diminishing returns to particular ideas, but says it has no strong view on whether progress with humans researching as they do now accelerates or slows. It does not attribute an expected slowdown to exhaustion of low-hanging fruit.

r002.rationale: It says AI research systems could increase effective research and improve AI further, but does not state that expanding the research workforce offsets the growing difficulty of finding improvements.

r003.rationale: The response gives no estimate of training-compute improvement or a three-to-four-orders-of-magnitude figure.
